title: Accounting firms are racing to use AI. Most still lack the infrastructure to make it work, according to a new report.
excerpt: Accounting firms are racing to prove they can use AI. A new report from Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting found that their infrastructure can't keep up.
content_html:
By Polly Thompson

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-22T09:45:01.335Z

Accountants are proving to be an unlikely case study in how AI is changing the workplace.

The profession's formulaic, data-heavy workload has meant firms have been quick to adopt the technology, and it is frequently cited as one of the industries most at risk of AI job displacement.

A new report shows that the accounting industry is also emblematic of another key AI development: the great hype-versus-reality debate.

Enthusiasm for the technology is outpacing firms' ability to embed it across their businesses, according to the Future Ready Accountant report, published by Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting on Wednesday.

The findings are based on responses from 746 US accounting professionals between June and July 2026. Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting sells software and tools to tax, accounting, and audit firms.

83% of US accounting firms identify as "technology innovators or early adopters," the report found. It defined "technology innovators" as those willing to test or adopt emerging technologies and solutions ahead of peers.

On that measure, accounting firms are moving quickly: 88% of US professionals said they use generative AI for daily work, and 68% said the same for agentic AI.

What US accounting firms aren't achieving is a sophisticated tech infrastructure to back up their appetite for the new technology, according to the study.

Only 13% of firms assessed for their digital maturity met the requirements for what Wolters Kluwer called "a tech-forward threshold," which refers to the actual operating environment firms have created.

To achieve a tech-forward threshold, an accounting firm must use AI regularly, be fully cloud-based, or have a defined plan to become fully cloud-based, and meet a high technology-integration threshold.

Not every respondent was evaluated for digital maturity — 300 of the 746 responded to all the relevant questions — so the 83% and 13% figures are not directly comparable. But the results do point to a familiar AI problem: companies can roll out individual tools without connecting the data, workflows, and systems that would allow those tools to reshape how work actually gets done.

While US firms have built significant momentum in technology adoption, they have yet to translate individual technologies into a more connected operating model, Wolters Kluwer told Business Insider.

"The gap is less about firms thinking they are more advanced than they really are and more about the distinction between adopting technology and integrating it across the business," a spokesperson said.

The distinction matters in an industry as ripe for AI disruption as accounting. AI can easily take on repetitive tasks such as extracting and cleaning financial data, reconciling accounts, drafting reports, and flagging audit risks.

Senior executives tend to say that the shift makes accounting work more exciting and people-focused. It will free up junior accountants to work on more engaging tasks that would previously have been the responsibility of managers, while more senior workers help drive new business, they say.

Ensuring big operational change, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes, is the next challenge, the report said.
